title: The 10 best knowledge base software in 2026
summary: Compare 10 knowledge base platforms by AI search, governance, integrations, and analytics to pick the right wiki or help center.
body_markdown:
**If I had to cut this list down fast, I’d sort the tools by use case first:** internal wiki, support help center, data-linked portal, or Q&A knowledge hub. That’s the main split in this roundup of **10 tools** .


Here’s the short version:


- **[Jet Admin](https://jetadmin.io/)** fits teams that need[portals tied to live company data](https://www.jetadmin.io/blog/customer-portal-software-how-to-design-build-and-launch-a-secure-self-service-experience/) , strict access rules, and audit trails.
- **[Notion](https://www.notion.com/) ,[Confluence](https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence) , and[Slab](https://slab.com/)** fit internal docs and team wikis.
- **[Zendesk Guide](https://support.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/4408823954970-Welcome-to-Guide-for-help-center) ,[Document360](https://document360.com/) ,[Help Scout](https://www.helpscout.com/) , and[Helpjuice](https://helpjuice.com/)** lean toward support content and self-service.
- **[Guru](https://www.getguru.com/) and[Bloomfire](https://bloomfire.com/)** focus more on trusted answers, expert review, and searchable Q&A.
- The main things compared are **AI search, governance, integrations, and analytics** .


A few patterns stand out right away:


- If you need **deep permissions** , the list points more toward **Jet Admin, Confluence, Document360, and Zendesk Guide** .
- If you care most about **analytics** , **Document360** and **Helpjuice** get the most direct callouts.
- If your team already lives in one software stack, tools like **Confluence** and **Zendesk Guide** make more sense inside those ecosystems.
- If your content is spread across files, apps, and media, **Slab** and **Bloomfire** stand out for search.


## The 8 Best Knowledge Base Tools for Smarter Team Documentation

If I were choosing, I’d start with one question: **Do you need a wiki, a help center, or a[portal on top of live data](https://www.jetadmin.io/blog/customer-portal-software-how-to-design-build-and-launch-a-secure-self-service-experience/amp/) ?** That one choice removes half the list right away.


## 1.[Jet Admin](https://jetadmin.io/)


For teams that want a knowledge base linked to live business data, **Jet Admin** takes a data-first path. Instead of asking you to move everything into a new system, it connects to the data sources you already use. It then builds one unified data model across those sources, maps table relationships for you, and turns that content into[white-labeled portals](https://www.jetadmin.io/customer-portal) for IT, Operations, Product, and RevOps teams.


### AI search


Jet Admin’s **AI Co-builder** turns plain-language prompts into apps, pages, and automations while respecting each user’s permissions.


That matters because this kind of flexibility can fall apart fast if access gets sloppy.


### Governance


Jet Admin supports row-, field-, component-, and API-level permissions, along with SSO,[SAML](https://docs.oasis-open.org/security/saml/Post2.0/sstc-saml-tech-overview-2.0.html) , audit logs, and approval workflows. It also includes an admin-managed app catalog to cut down on tool sprawl, while **[Jet Bridge](https://docs.jetadmin.io/jet-bridge-deployment/jet-admin)** secures browser access to private databases.


### Integrations


Jet Admin connects with major databases, SaaS tools, file storage, and APIs. It also supports cloud, self-hosted, on-premise, and air-gapped deployments.


Those connections do more than link systems together. They also support reporting without copying data into another layer.


### Analytics


Jet Admin builds dashboards directly on connected data sources, with query builder support, computed columns, and real-time access. That setup works well for operational reporting across support and revenue teams.


## 2.[Notion](https://www.notion.com/)


For teams that want a workspace-first knowledge base, **Notion** puts speed and flexibility ahead of deep admin controls. It’s a solid pick for team wikis and internal documentation, especially when your team wants docs, notes, and day-to-day work in the same place.


### AI search


Notion AI can search wiki pages, databases, and connected apps. But there’s a catch: results depend a lot on how cleanly the workspace is set up. If pages have messy names, live in odd places, or get buried under too many layers, search quality drops.


### Governance


Notion includes page-level sharing, workspace permissions, and version history for tracking changes. That gives teams a decent level of control for everyday use. On Enterprise plans, admin controls get stronger.


### Integrations


Notion connects with common workplace tools and tends to work best when teams keep docs, tasks, and reference material in one workspace. When everything lives together, the system feels smoother and easier to use.


### Analytics


Notion has limited native analytics, so it fits documentation better than support reporting or knowledge-base performance tracking. Its strong point is fast internal documentation. Its weak point is operational oversight.


## 3.[Confluence](https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence)


For engineering and product teams already using Atlassian tools, Confluence is a strong fit for technical docs, release notes, and change tracking. It works best when documentation and issue tracking live in the same workflow.


That’s the main appeal here. If your team runs on Jira, Confluence fits naturally. If you want a standalone knowledge base, it’s usually not the best pick.


### AI search


Confluence uses **[Atlassian Intelligence](https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/use-cases/wiki)** to provide natural language search across spaces. Users can ask more complex questions and get synthesized answers based on existing documentation.


That helps with discovery. But the bigger story for many companies is access control, which is where Confluence feels more ready for large teams.


### Governance


Confluence supports site-, space-, and page-level permissions. It also supports SSO via SAML and OpenID Connect.


In plain English: teams can control who sees what at several layers, instead of relying on one broad permission setting.


### Integrations


Its strongest integration is Jira. It links specs, change requests, and release notes directly to tickets.


For Jira-centered teams, that connection can save a lot of back-and-forth. A spec doesn’t have to sit off in a separate system with no tie to the actual work item.


### Analytics


Not a highlighted strength.


## 4.[Guru](https://www.getguru.com/)


Guru is built around **verified, expert-owned answers** . It tends to fit best when trusted answers matter more than broad workspace flexibility.


### AI search


Guru's AI search, **Guru Answers** , returns cited responses from expert-owned Cards, so teams can verify information quickly. That setup also keeps knowledge modular, which makes updates simpler when something changes.


### Governance


Guru's Card-based ownership model makes it straightforward to review and update individual pieces of information without touching unrelated content. Instead of reworking a big page every time one detail shifts, teams can update the specific Card that owns that answer.


### Integrations


Integration details are not available from the source material.

That makes Guru a strong fit for teams that care most about trusted answers, not deep admin controls.


## 5.[Document360](https://document360.com/)


Document360 is built for teams that need a structured knowledge base, tight publishing control, and clear data on how each article performs.


### AI search


Document360 includes AI-powered search that surfaces relevant articles from natural language queries. That means users can type what they need in plain English and get useful answers without digging through category trees.


### Governance


Document360 supports role-based access control, draft and review workflows, and version history. For content managers, that translates into clear control over what goes live, who can edit, and how changes are tracked over time.


### Integrations


Document360 connects with help desk tools, chat platforms, and analytics services. So if your team wants the knowledge base tied into current support workflows, it fits in without much friction.


### Analytics


Document360 provides article-level performance data, including views, search terms, and failed searches. This gives teams a direct way to spot content gaps and decide which updates matter most based on actual usage.


## 6.[Zendesk Guide](https://support.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/4408823954970-Welcome-to-Guide-for-help-center)


Zendesk Guide is the knowledge base part of Zendesk. It’s built for support teams that want self-service articles linked straight to ticketing.


### AI search


Zendesk AI suggests relevant articles and helps deflect common requests before they ever reach an agent.


### Governance


Guide supports **SSO via SAML and OpenID Connect** . It also offers domain-based access restrictions, so only users from approved domains can get into the portal.


### Integrations


Its closest tie is with Zendesk’s own ticketing system. That keeps self-service content and support requests in the same Zendesk workspace, which makes day-to-day support a lot simpler.


### Analytics


It tracks ticket deflection and CSAT.

## 9.[Slab](https://slab.com/)


If your team wants a simple internal wiki without a lot of admin work, Slab fits that lane well. It’s built for team documentation and keeps the setup pretty light.


### AI search


Slab’s standout feature is **Unified Search** . It pulls results from Slab’s own wiki and linked tools like Slack, GitHub, Jira, and Google Drive. So instead of bouncing between apps, your team can search across Slab and those connected tools in one place.


### Governance


Slab organizes content into **Topics** instead of old-school folders. Permissions are set at the Topic level, with access controlled by Topic, group, or user.


It also comes with three main roles:


- **Admin**
- **Member**
- **Guest**


Slab also includes content verification to help keep pages current. The setup is simple, which helps teams manage access without a lot of extra admin work.


### Integrations


Slab connects with Slack, GitHub, Jira, and Google Drive. Most of these connections feed into **Unified Search** , which is where they do most of their work.

## 10.[Bloomfire](https://bloomfire.com/)


Bloomfire works well for teams that want to turn employee Q&A into a searchable knowledge base. It puts Q&A at the center: employees ask questions, and subject matter experts provide verified answers. That makes it a stronger fit for teams trying to keep institutional knowledge from day-to-day conversations, not just store static docs.


### AI search


Bloomfire’s **Deep Search** indexes every word in every file, including text inside PDFs, Word documents, and PowerPoint files. It also transcribes video and audio files on its own, so both spoken and written content can show up in search results.

## Which tool fits your use case


After comparing features, use this checklist to match a tool to your workflow and control needs. The goal is simple: pick the option that fits how your team works and the level of control you need day to day. For structured internal documentation tied to live data, **Jet Admin** stands out because it brings together governance, authentication, audit logs, and flexible deployment.


Use the checks below to narrow the list fast.


- **AI answer quality** → Does it give accurate answers based on your content?
- **Source citation** → Can people verify where the answer came from?
- **Review ownership** → Is someone clearly responsible for reviews, and is stale content flagged?
- **SSO and SAML support** → Are SSO and SAML included in the plan you need?
- **Audit logs** → Do logs track views, edits, and exports?
- **Data retention and export** → Can you keep and export content cleanly?
- **Integration depth** → Do the integrations support your core workflows?
- **Plan-level limits** → Are caps on users, workspaces, or API usage workable for your team?


Choose the tool that passes these checks with the least compromise.


## FAQs


### How do I choose between a wiki, help center, and data-linked portal?


Choose based on your main goal:


- **Wiki** : knowledge management, team collaboration, and long-form documentation
- **Help center** : customer-facing support, self-service, and external access
- **Data-linked portal** : operational workflows, billing, or real-time data


A wiki works best when you need flexible, searchable documents. A help center is made for support. A data-linked portal is the right fit when users need to work with live data, not just read static content.


### Which features matter most for enterprise knowledge base software?


The most important features are **security** , governance, and data integration. Look for granular role-based access controls, **SSO** , audit trails, version history, and compliance support such as[SOC 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_and_Organization_Controls) or[GDPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Data_Protection_Regulation) .


Enterprise platforms should also connect directly to existing databases and SaaS tools. On top of that, they should support automated workflows and AI-assisted search, so information stays accurate and easy to find as teams and data grow.


### What should I test before committing to a knowledge base tool?


Test your most critical workflows with **actual data** instead of polished demos. That’s how you see whether the relational logic holds up, how the system performs under normal load, and whether it fits your migration plans. It also helps to look closely at document volume and what your power users will need day to day.


Check the basics early so you don’t get surprised later:


- Support for the connectors you rely on
- **SSO**
- Granular permissions
- Security certifications such as SOC 2 or[HIPAA](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/covered-entities/index.html)


Then look at total cost of ownership over the next two to three years. That means more than license fees. Factor in seats, admin time, and training too.
